title: Bigger beetles take over. Then what?
hook: Large beetles out-breed small ones in every meeting. Is the population better off?

knows: fitness depends on whom you meet (strategy-builder)
doesNotKnow: that a strategy can invade and become stable even though everyone ends up with less

misconception: Evolution makes a population better off on average.
objective: The learner can explain that large beetles out-score small ones against either opponent, so they spread from 1% to 99% (by generation 24) and cannot be invaded by small mutants, yet the all-large population averages 4 offspring where the all-small one averaged 6.

claims.text: With these payoffs (surviving offspring per meeting: small vs small 6, small vs large 2, large vs small 8, large vs large 4), large scores more than small whatever the mix: 8 > 6 against small and 4 > 2 against large.
claims.source: With large share x: large 8(1 − x) + 4x, small 6(1 − x) + 2x; the difference is 2 at every x. Demo.tsx wL/wS. Our own payoffs, not the book's. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. wL - wS = 2 at every x (8-6 = 4-2 = 2); Demo.tsx wL/wS.

claims.text: In the stage's update rule (payoff = surviving offspring, no baseline; share x' = x·W_large / mean W), large rises from 1% to 99% by generation 24 (4.1% at 5, 16.3% at 10, 93.1% at 20); the curve is marked '99% at gen 24'.
claims.source: Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14 (deterministic, no random seed): 0.0415 at 5, 0.1633 at 10, 0.9306 at 20, first ≥ 0.99 at generation 24 (0.9947). The no-baseline choice matters: with a baseline of 10 offspring the same climb takes 69 generations, so the stage says 'no baseline'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Re-ran Demo.tsx next(): 0.0415 at 5, 0.1633 at 10, 0.9306 at 20, 0.9896 at 23, first >= 0.99 at 24 (0.9947). Baseline 10 gives 69, as stated. | REWORDED v2 (builder, 2026-10-14): Adds the on-stage mark (first generation with share >= 0.99, computed from the learner's run). Builder re-run: first gen >= 0.99 is 24. Unverified.

claims.text: An all-small population averages 6 offspring per meeting; an all-large population averages 4.
claims.source: Small vs small = 6, large vs large = 4. The stage readout shows 6.0 at generation 0 (1% large gives 5.98) and 4.0 from generation 24 on (4.01). Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. avg(0.01) = 5.98, avg at gen 24 = 4.01, at 30 = 4.000.

claims.text: Once nearly all beetles are large, a small mutant scores about 2 where a large one scores about 4, so small mutants shrink back: on the stage, turning 5% small at generation 30 (mutants 2.2 vs 4.2) leaves 99.8% large five generations later (shown as 100%).
claims.source: Payoffs from c1; builder's Node run, 2026-10-14: from 0.9499 large (5% turned small at generation 30) the share is 0.9731, 0.9860, then 0.9929 (back above 0.99) after 3 generations. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. From 0.9499 at gen 30: 0.9731, 0.9860, 0.9929 (back above 0.99 after 3 generations). Near all-large, wS = 2.0003, wL = 4.0003. | REWORDED v2 (builder, 2026-10-14): Now shown: 'Turn 5% small, run 5' dips and steps 5 generations. Builder node re-run of the Demo update rule: x30 = 0.99992, dipped 0.94992 (small 2.20, large 4.20), then 97.31, 98.60, 99.29, 99.64, 99.82%. Unverified.

claims.text: An evolutionarily stable strategy is one that, once common, cannot be invaded by a small group of mutants using another strategy.
claims.source: Maynard Smith J. & Price G.R. (1973) The logic of animal conflict, Nature 246:15-18; Easley & Kleinberg (2010) Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 7 (section unconfirmed). Attribution: fact-checker to confirm. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Definition matches Maynard Smith & Price (1973) as reported by Wikipedia (ESS) and Sandholm's EGT notes (resistant to invasion by a small group of mutants), via web search; papers not opened. Easley & Kleinberg ch. 7 is 'Evolutionary Game Theory' (confirmed from knowledge and an MIT syllabus listing EK ch. 7 for ESS); ESS is defined in 7.2 from my knowledge of the book, section not opened. Also checked the stage's game is an ESS: large vs large 4 > small vs large 2.

claims.text: The model is a toy: chosen payoffs, no baseline offspring, random meetings in a very large population; it is not a claim about real beetles.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx, stated on the stage and in the reveal. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Stage and reveal say so (Demo.tsx 'Score = surviving offspring, no baseline. Beetles meet at random.' and the muted reveal line).

recall.question: A trait wins against every opponent, spreads to the whole population, and leaves everyone with fewer offspring than before. What does this show?
options: A stable strategy need not make the population better off
The trait must have been unstable
The population must have shrunk first
recall.why: Selection compares a strategy with its rivals, not with the population's old average. Large beetles out-score small ones in every meeting, so they take over and resist invasion, even though all-large averages 4 where all-small averaged 6.
